analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover preexisting conditions and expands Medicaid and subsidized private insurance.
analysis.headline: Became law on March 23, 2010 after the Senate passed it 60-39 and the House accepted the Senate version 219-212, with no Republican votes on either final tally.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill began as a small tax bill for military homebuyers and became the Affordable Care Act. It bans health plans from denying or dropping coverage for preexisting conditions, ends lifetime and annual dollar limits, requires free preventive care, lets young adults stay on a parent's plan until 26, expands Medicaid to nearly everyone under 65 with income up to 133% of the poverty line, and gives refundable tax credits to households earning up to 400% of poverty to buy private plans. To pay for it, it fines most people who go without coverage and large employers that don't offer it, raises the Medicare payroll tax on income over $200,000 ($250,000 for couples), and charges annual fees to health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and medical device makers.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured people gain the most: people with preexisting conditions can no longer be denied or dropped, low-income adults gain Medicaid, working households up to 400% of poverty get premium subsidies and out-of-pocket caps, young adults up to 26 can stay on a parent's plan, Medicare beneficiaries get a discount on drugs in the coverage gap and free preventive visits, and small firms get a tax credit of up to 50% of coverage costs. Private insurers also gain a large, mandated, federally subsidized customer base, and Members of Congress and staff are moved onto plans created under the law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Health plans may no longer impose preexisting condition exclusions or discriminate based on health status, and premiums may vary only by age, location, tobacco use, and family size.

Medicaid is extended to individuals under 65 with incomes at or below 133% of the federal poverty line starting in 2014, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of newly eligible people from 2014 to 2016.
Households with income between 100% and 400% of poverty receive refundable tax credits for private premiums and reduced out-of-pocket maximums.

Plans are barred from lifetime or annual dollar limits and from rescinding coverage except for fraud, must cover recommended preventive services with no cost sharing, and must cover unmarried adult children until age 26.

Insurers must rebate premiums to enrollees if they spend less than 85% of premium revenue (80% in small-group and individual markets) on clinical care and quality improvement, and hospitals must publish their standard charges.
Small employers with up to 25 workers averaging under $50,000 in pay can claim a tax credit for 50% of employee health coverage costs.
Medicare Part D gains a manufacturer discount program for the coverage gap and a $500 increase in the initial coverage limit, and Medicare adds a free annual wellness visit with no cost sharing.

The 340B drug discount program is expanded to children's hospitals, cancer hospitals, critical access, rural referral, and sole community hospitals, letting them buy outpatient and inpatient drugs at discounted prices.

analysis.who_pays: People who remain uninsured pay a penalty starting in 2014, though low-income people, tribes, hardship cases, and others are exempt. Employers with more than 50 full-time workers face fines if they don't offer coverage or impose long waiting periods. Individuals earning over $200,000 and couples over $250,000 pay an additional 0.9% Medicare payroll tax, higher Medicare Part D premiums, and face a higher threshold for deducting medical expenses. Health insurers, brand-name prescription drug manufacturers, and medical device makers pay new annual fees, and indoor tanning services carry a 10% excise tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Uninsured individuals, large employers, high earners

drawbacks.text: The law requires most individuals to maintain minimum essential coverage beginning in 2014 and imposes a penalty on those who do not, exempting low-income people who cannot afford it, members of Indian tribes, religious objectors, and hardship cases.

It imposes fines on large employers with more than 50 full-time employees that fail to offer coverage or impose waiting periods longer than 60 days, and requires employers with more than 200 workers to automatically enroll new employees.

The hospital insurance tax rate rises by 0.9% for individual taxpayers earning over $200,000 ($250,000 for joint filers) after 2012, and Part D enrollees above income thresholds must pay higher premiums.

The Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act creates a biosimilar approval pathway but bars the FDA from approving a biosimilar as effective until 12 years after the original brand biologic was licensed, delaying lower-priced competition for over a decade.

Plans in existence on enactment day are 'grandfathered' and exempt from many of the new market rules even if they renew existing enrollees, and collectively bargained plans are exempt until the agreements terminate.

New annual fees are imposed on health insurance providers, on branded prescription drug manufacturers, and on medical device makers, which fund the coverage expansion but represent new costs on regulated industries.
States may ban abortion coverage in plans sold on their exchanges, and federal funds may not be used for abortion services, requiring separate accounts for such payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage gains are large and concrete: millions of people who could be denied, dropped, or priced out of insurance gain protected access, and the Medicaid expansion plus subsidies cover the population least able to afford care. The trade-offs are real. People who stay uninsured face a fine, high earners pay new taxes, employers face new penalties, and brand drug makers won a 12-year monopoly on follow-on biologics that keeps cheaper competition off the market for years. The law also entrenches private insurers as the permanent channel for subsidized coverage — it imposes an individual mandate, routes new tax credits through private plans, and includes no public insurance option — so the same law that protects patients also guarantees the industry a larger, federally funded customer base.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed a small military tax bill 416-0, the Senate stripped out its contents and inserted the full health care overhaul, passed it 60-39 on December 24, 2009, and the House accepted the Senate version 219-212 on March 21, 2010, with President Obama signing it two days later.

narrative.text: Introduced in the House on September 17, 2009 as the Service Members Home Ownership Tax Act of 2009, a bill amending the first-time homebuyer tax credit and corporate estimated tax payments.
The House passed it 416-0 on October 8, 2009 under suspension of the rules, with 243 of 255 voting Democrats and 173 of 177 voting Republicans in favor.
The Senate used this House tax bill as the vehicle for the health care overhaul: a motion to cut off debate on proceeding to the bill passed exactly 60-39 on November 21, 2009, the minimum needed.

Senate Republicans repeatedly moved to send the bill back to the Finance Committee with instructions — via Senator McCain four times and Senators Hatch, Johanns, and Crapo once each — and every motion failed on near party-line votes between December 3 and December 15, 2009.

Senator Reid moved to commit the bill to the Finance Committee with instructions to report the Manager's amendment (SA 3280), which fell when cloture was invoked on a related amendment on December 21, 2009.

Cloture was invoked 60-39 on December 23, 2009, and the Senate passed the amended bill 60-39 on December 24, 2009, with all 58 Democrats, the one Independent Democrat, and the one Independent voting yes and all 39 voting Republicans opposed; one senator did not vote.

The version that passed the Senate included a provision setting the federal Medicaid match for Nebraska at 100% of the cost of newly eligible residents beginning in 2017, while other states received lower matching rates.
The House agreed to the Senate amendments on March 21, 2010 by a recorded vote of 219-212: all 178 Republicans voted no, along with 34 of 253 voting Democrats; 219 Democrats voted yes.
The bill was presented to the President on March 22, signed on March 23, 2010, and became Public Law 111-148.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill became law, the people who came out ahead are the previously uninsured, people with preexisting conditions, and low- and moderate-income households who gained coverage protections, Medicaid, and subsidies. Private health insurers also came out well ahead: the individual mandate and new federal subsidies steer millions of customers into private plans, with no public insurance alternative, even as the industry accepted new fees and rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insured millions; private insurers gained customers.

sides.party_line_note: The fight split almost entirely by party: the House passed the original bill 416-0 with no opposition, but final passage fell along party lines — 219-212 in the House (zero Republicans, 34 Democratic defections) and 60-39 in the Senate (every Democrat and Independent yes, every voting Republican no) — with Republicans' only Senate tactic, repeated motions to recommit, failing on near party-line votes.

industries.note: The law bans preexisting-condition denials, rescissions, and lifetime limits, requires medical loss ratio rebates, subjects premium increases to federal and state review, and imposes an annual fee on insurers. But it also requires nearly everyone to carry coverage and pays new subsidies through private plans, making insurers the permanent, federally funded channel for health coverage with no public alternative.

Drug makers pay an annual fee on branded sales and higher Medicaid rebates, but the law gives biologic follow-on products 12 years of market exclusivity before cheaper biosimilars can be approved, protecting brand biologic revenue. The Part D coverage-gap discount program and 340B expansion cut into pricing on those channels.

Hospitals gain tens of millions of insured patients but absorb Medicare payment reductions, productivity adjustments, readmission penalties, DSH cuts tied to falling uninsured rates, price transparency requirements, and new charity-care rules for tax-exempt hospitals. Rural and critical access hospitals receive extended payment protections.
Device manufacturers pay a new annual fee on gross sales over $5 million, while broader insurance coverage increases the pool of patients able to afford their products.

Employers with more than 50 full-time workers face fines for not offering coverage or imposing long waiting periods, and those with 200-plus workers must auto-enroll staff, though small firms get a 50% tax credit for covering low-wage workers.

New physician-owned hospitals without a Medicare provider agreement by August 1, 2010 are barred from Medicare participation, limiting physician investment in hospitals that lawmakers saw as self-dealing, with narrow exceptions for rural facilities.

Individuals earning over $200,000 and couples over $250,000 pay an added 0.9% Medicare tax and higher Part D premiums, and the threshold for deducting medical expenses rises from 7.5% to 10% of income.
A 10% excise tax is imposed on indoor tanning services starting July 1, 2010, exempting medical phototherapy.
